messages.content:
# Quantization lit review - sci fair 2027
Last edited 2026-11-12

## Goal
Run a 7B chat model on my 16GB MacBook using <6GB RAM with minimal quality loss.
Project needs a defensible comparison, not just "it felt fine".

## Options compared

### 1. GPTQ 4-bit (Frantar et al.)
- Needs calibration data (128 samples from C4)
- Built for GPU; Metal/CPU support is weak
- Perplexity (wikitext2): 5.85 vs fp16 5.68
- Quantize time: ~35 min on borrowed RTX box (Priya's)
- Size: 3.9 GB
- Verdict: good numbers, bad fit for my laptop

### 2. AWQ 4-bit (Lin et al.)
- Protects ~1% salient weights using activation stats
- Perplexity: 5.78
- Also GPU-first; no clean Metal path as of Oct
- Size: 3.9 GB
- Verdict: best 4-bit quality on paper, same laptop problem

### 3. GGUF Q4_K_M (llama.cpp)
- Mixed 4/6-bit blocks, no calibration needed
- Perplexity: 5.80 (my own run)
- Speed on M2: 22 tok/s
- Size: 4.1 GB
- Verdict: runs natively, best speed/size tradeoff

### 4. GGUF Q5_K_M
- Perplexity: 5.73 (my own run)
- Speed on M2: 18 tok/s
- Size: 4.8 GB
- Verdict: closest to fp16, still under budget

## Numbers table
| method   | size GB | wikitext2 ppl | tok/s M2 |
|----------|---------|---------------|----------|
| fp16     | 13.5    | 5.68          | 9 (swaps)|
| GPTQ 4b  | 3.9     | 5.85          | n/a      |
| AWQ 4b   | 3.9     | 5.78          | n/a      |
| Q4_K_M   | 4.1     | 5.80          | 22       |
| Q5_K_M   | 4.8     | 5.73          | 18       |

## Decision (Nov 12)
Go with Q4_K_M as the main config, keep Q5_K_M as the quality comparison.
Drop GPTQ/AWQ from the experiments, but cite them in background.

## Caveats
- GPTQ and AWQ ppl numbers are copied from the papers at ctx 2048
- My GGUF runs used ctx 4096 -> NOT apples to apples
- Only tested on wikitext2, no task benchmarks yet

## Citations to chase
- Frantar et al. 2023 GPTQ - need venue + page numbers
- Lin et al. 2024 AWQ - check which version I read (v2?)
- llama.cpp k-quants discussion thread - find a stable link, maybe archive it

## TODO
- [ ] Rerun GGUF ppl at ctx 2048 so it matches the papers
- [ ] Add one task benchmark (HellaSwag subset, 500 q)
- [ ] Get Mr. Okafor to sign off on methods by Dec 4
- [ ] Draft poster section 2 (methods)
- [x] Measure RAM use for Q4_K_M (5.2 GB peak)

submitting my microplastics-in-creek paper to the tri-county young scholars thing. can you read the guidelines page and tell me what i actually need to do + when? https://www.tcscholars.example.org/symposium/2027/guidelines

messages.name: fetch_url
messages.content:
Tri-County Young Scholars Symposium 2027 - Paper Submission Guidelines
Last updated: April 12, 2027

1. ELIGIBILITY
- Open to students currently enrolled in grades 9-12 at schools in Alder, Brenton, or Calloway County.
- Individual or team (max 3 authors) submissions.
- Work must be original and not previously published.
- Each submission needs one adult mentor (teacher, professor, or professional).

2. KEY DATES
- Abstract registration opens: March 1
- Abstract due: May 15, 11:59 pm ET
- Full paper due: June 1, 11:59 pm ET
- Mentor letter due: June 1, 11:59 pm ET
- Finalist notification: June 20
- Symposium (Calloway Community College): July 11
- Late submissions are not accepted. No extensions.

3. ABSTRACT
- 250 words maximum.
- Must include research question, method, and main finding.
- Abstract can be revised until the full paper deadline, but registration is required by May 15.

4. FULL PAPER FORMAT
- Maximum 3,500 words, excluding references, figure captions, and appendices.
- 12 pt serif font, double spaced, 1 inch margins.
- PDF only. Maximum file size 10 MB.
- Title page with title, author names, school, and mentor name. No school logos.
- Maximum 6 figures and 4 tables in the main text.
- Page numbers required, bottom center.

5. CITATIONS
- APA 7th edition for in-text citations and the reference list.
- Minimum 8 references, at least 5 must be peer-reviewed.
- Websites and preprints are allowed but must include access dates.
- Uncited figures or data will be disqualified.

6. HUMAN AND ANIMAL SUBJECTS
- Any survey or interview of people requires Form H-2 signed by a teacher or school administrator.
- Vertebrate animal work requires Form A-1.
- Environmental sampling on public land does not require a form, but you must list the sampling location and permit status, if any, in the methods section.

7. DATA AVAILABILITY
- Include a one-paragraph data availability statement.
- Raw data should be uploaded as a CSV (optional, but scored under Reproducibility).

8. SCORING RUBRIC (100 points)
- Research question and significance: 20
- Methods and rigor: 30
- Analysis and results: 25
- Writing and organization: 15
- Reproducibility and data: 10

9. FILE NAMING
- Use LastName_FirstName_SchoolCode_Title.pdf
- Example: Rivera_Ana_BHS_SoilPH.pdf
- Team papers use the first author's name.

10. SUBMISSION
- Submit through the portal at tcscholars.example.org/portal.
- Create one account per team.
- Mentor receives a separate link to upload the letter.
- Confirmation email arrives within 24 hours. If you do not get it, contact submissions@tcscholars.example.org.

11. FEES
- Registration fee is $15 per submission.
- Fee waiver available for students on free or reduced lunch; request through your counselor before May 10.

12. QUESTIONS
- Email info@tcscholars.example.org. Replies within 3 business days.

Biggest thing: the abstract is due May 15 (a week from today), and you must register by then even though you can edit it later. Full paper and mentor letter are both due June 1, no extensions.

Paper requirements: PDF under 10 MB, max 3,500 words, 12 pt double spaced, APA 7, at least 8 references (5 peer-reviewed), max 6 figures/4 tables, named LastName_FirstName_SchoolCode_Title.pdf. Since it's creek sampling, no human-subjects form is needed, but state the sampling location and permit status in methods and add a data availability paragraph. The fee is $15, and a waiver request must go through your counselor by May 10, which is in two days. Finalists hear back June 20.

messages.name: fetch_url
messages.content:
SQLite WAL explained
Posted 2025-08-14 by J. Okonkwo

In WAL mode, writes are appended to a separate -wal file instead of modifying the database directly. Readers keep reading from a consistent snapshot, so many readers can run while one writer writes. Only one writer is allowed at a time. A checkpoint periodically copies WAL content back into the main database file. WAL does not work reliably over network filesystems because it relies on shared memory (-shm).

quick q for AP Calc BC, is the series sum of 1/(n ln n) from n=2 to infinity convergent? my teacher said use integral test but I blanked

It diverges. Use the integral test on f(x) = 1/(x ln x), which is positive, continuous, and decreasing for x ≥ 2.

∫ from 2 to ∞ of dx/(x ln x): let u = ln x, du = dx/x, so you get ∫ du/u = ln|u|. Evaluated, that's ln(ln b) − ln(ln 2) as b → ∞, which goes to infinity.

Since the integral diverges, the series diverges too. It's a classic example of a series that diverges very slowly.
ok and what about 1/(n (ln n)^2)

That one converges. Same substitution u = ln x gives ∫ du/u² = −1/u. From ln 2 to ∞ that evaluates to 1/ln 2, which is finite.

So by the integral test, the series sum of 1/(n (ln n)²) from n=2 converges. The extra power on the log is what flips it, similar to how p-series change behavior at p = 1.

git question. I committed to main by accident but I meant to be on a feature branch, haven't pushed yet. how do I move the commit over

Create the branch at your current commit, then move main back one commit:

git branch feature/my-thing
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git checkout feature/my-thing

The branch keeps your commit, and main goes back to where it was. The reset --hard only discards uncommitted changes in your working tree, so stash anything unsaved first. If you committed more than one, use HEAD~2 and so on.
nice, and if I have uncommitted stuff too?

Run git stash first, do the steps above, then git stash pop on the feature branch. Alternatively, git switch -c feature/my-thing before anything else carries uncommitted changes along, and then you can reset main with git branch -f main origin/main.

quick q for my lit review, what's the difference between a systematic review and a meta-analysis? people keep using them like they're the same thing

They're related but not the same.

- Systematic review: a structured, reproducible search and appraisal of all the studies on a question, using predefined inclusion criteria. The results can be summarized in words or tables.
- Meta-analysis: a statistical technique that pools numerical results from multiple studies into one combined effect estimate.

A meta-analysis is often done as part of a systematic review, when the studies are similar enough to combine. But a systematic review doesn't need a meta-analysis, and a meta-analysis done on a non-systematic sample of studies is weaker because of selection bias.
ok so can I cite a systematic review without meta-analysis as evidence of effect size?

Only loosely. Without pooling, there is no single combined effect size, so you can only report the range or direction of effects across studies, for example "most included trials found a modest positive effect." If you need a number, cite a review that includes a meta-analysis, or cite the individual studies' effect sizes directly. State clearly which one you're doing.

quick q for my stats project, if my p-value is 0.06 can i say the result is significant? and whats the difference between that and effect size

At the usual 0.05 cutoff, p = 0.06 is not statistically significant. Say you failed to reject the null, not that there's no effect. You can report the exact p-value and note it's close to the threshold.

The p-value tells you how surprising your data would be if there were no real effect. Effect size tells you how big the difference or relationship is (for example Cohen's d or r). A tiny effect can have a small p with a huge sample, and a large effect can have p = 0.06 with a small sample, so report both.

why does ['1','2','3'].map(parseInt) give [1, NaN, NaN]?? js is gaslighting me

map passes three arguments to its callback: the item, the index and the array. parseInt takes (string, radix), so it receives the index as the radix. The calls are effectively parseInt('1', 0), parseInt('2', 1) and parseInt('3', 2). Radix 0 falls back to base 10, so you get 1. Radix 1 is invalid, so you get NaN. In base 2 the digit '3' doesn't exist, so that's NaN too.
lol ok whats the cleanest fix
Use `['1','2','3'].map(Number)`, which ignores the extra arguments. If you want parseInt, wrap it and pass the radix explicitly: `.map(s => parseInt(s, 10))`.

quick q for my AP Gov FRQ, whats the difference between federalism's 'dual' and 'cooperative' models? need like 2 sentences i can remember

Dual federalism ("layer cake") means national and state governments operate in separate, distinct spheres with little overlap. Cooperative federalism ("marble cake") means they share responsibilities and work together, often through federal grants and mandates, as with Medicaid or highway funding.

Dual: the pre-New Deal era, where states handled most domestic matters like education and commerce within their borders. Cooperative: the Medicaid program, where the federal government funds part of the cost and states administer it under federal rules. For extra credit on an FRQ, you can also cite No Child Left Behind or the Affordable Care Act as cooperative examples.

quick q, if I study 45 min then take a 10 min break, how many full study blocks fit between 3:30pm and 8:00pm? dinner isn't until after 8

From 3:30 to 8:00 is 270 minutes. Each block plus break is 55 minutes, so 4 full cycles use 220 minutes (ending at 7:10). The remaining 50 minutes isn't enough for another full 45+10 cycle, but you can fit a fifth 45-minute study block (7:10 to 7:55) and skip the last break. So 5 study blocks total.

my common app essay opening is: "Ever since I was little, I have always loved fixing things." feels really generic. how do i make it better without being cringe

It's generic because it states a trait instead of showing it. Fixes:

- Start in a specific moment: "The toaster had been dead for three days when I took it apart on the garage floor."
- Swap the claim for a concrete detail (an object, a sound, a mistake).
- Cut "ever since I was little" and "always loved". Admissions readers see them constantly.
- Let the reader infer the trait. If the scene shows you fixing things, you never need to say it.

If you paste your next two or three sentences, I can suggest a specific rewrite.
ok what if i start with the time i fried my dad's old laptop trying to replace the fan

That's much better. A failure is more memorable and more honest than a success. Something like:

"The smell hit me before the screen went black: burnt plastic, and the end of my dad's ten-year-old laptop."

Then move quickly to what you did next (what you learned, how you fixed it or his reaction) so the essay turns into a story about how you handle mistakes, not just the mistake itself.

messages.content:
DRAFT: "Let Seniors Eat Off Campus Again" by Hana Alder
Reviewer: Ms. Okafor (journalism advisor) | Reviewed 2027-05-18 | Due to the Ledger: 2027-05-27
==========
[P1] Every day at 12:10, about 200 seniors file out of Brindle Hill's cafeteria and eat nothing.
[COMMENT] Strong hook, but "eat nothing" is an exaggeration. Do you have a number? Maybe survey a few seniors.
[P1] The open lunch policy ended in September 2026, and the cafeteria has been a ghost town ever since.
[COMMENT] Cite the source for the policy date (board minutes?). "Ghost town" contradicts your own line in P2.
[P2] Cafeteria sales are down 40 percent, according to a student I talked to.
[COMMENT] Not good enough. Ask the food service office for real figures, or cut the stat.
[P2] Meanwhile the lines for the three microwaves stretch past the vending machines.
[COMMENT] Nice detail. Keep.
[P3] The administration clearly thinks seniors are too immature to leave campus for 40 minutes.
[COMMENT] Tone is too snarky here. You are attributing a motive you can't prove.
[P3] Principal Hallworth said the change was about safety.
[COMMENT] Great that you included this, but it's one line. Give her argument a real paragraph.
[COMMENT] You mention "two incidents" last spring in passing. What were they? Check with the front office.
[P4] The principle has said she will not revisit the policy this year.
[COMMENT] principle -> principal. Also, is this a direct quote? Attribute it properly.
[P4] Other districts, like Maple Ridge, let seniors leave with a signed permission slip.
[COMMENT] Good comparison. Link or name a source for Maple Ridge's policy.
[P5] Students deserve to be trusted. It is time to bring open lunch back.
[COMMENT] Ending is weak and a bit generic. End on a concrete proposal (pilot program? permission slips?).
[P5] If the school can trust us with college-level classes, it can trust us with lunch.
[COMMENT] Love this line. Move it to the end.
----------
OVERALL COMMENTS
[COMMENT] Word count is about 940. The Ledger limit is 700, so cut 240 words.
[COMMENT] The piece is one-sided. A reader who supports the ban should still feel fairly represented.
[COMMENT] Add at least one direct quote from an administrator and one from a student.
[COMMENT] Voice is lively, which is your strength. Do not sand it off while cutting.
TODO LIST (from Ms. Okafor)
1. Verify or cut the 40 percent figure
2. Expand the safety counterargument and check the two incidents
3. Add two direct quotes
4. Tone down P3
5. Fix principal/principle and attribute the P4 quote
6. Cut to 700 words
7. New ending with a concrete proposal
Submit revised draft by Thu 2027-05-27.

Ms. Okafor likes your voice, the microwave-line detail, and the "college-level classes" line (move it to the end). Her fixes, in priority order:
- Content: verify the "40 percent" sales figure with food service or cut it. Give Principal Hallworth's safety argument a full paragraph and check what the "two incidents" were. Add one administrator quote and one student quote.
- Tone/accuracy: soften the P3 line about administrators thinking seniors are immature. Fix "principle" to "principal" in P4, attribute that quote, and source the Maple Ridge policy.
- Structure: cut about 240 words (940 to 700) and end on a concrete proposal like a pilot or permission slips.

The revised draft is due Thursday, May 27.

messages.content:
AP Literature & Composition - Period 3 - Ms. Okonkwo
Announcements and deadlines, Fall semester (last updated Nov 20)

== GENERAL ==
Room 214, A/B day schedule.
Office hours: Tue/Thu 7:15-7:45am, or by email.
Late work: -10% per day, max 3 days, then a zero.
Bring your annotated copy of Hamlet every class.
Turnitin class code is posted on the board.

== WEEK OF NOV 30 ==
Mon Nov 30: Hamlet Act 3 annotations due at start of class.
Wed Dec 2: Vocab unit 6 quiz (words 1-20).
Fri Dec 4: Timed write #3, prose analysis, in class (40 min).

== WEEK OF DEC 7 ==
Mon Dec 7: Finish Hamlet Act 4 reading.
Wed Dec 9: Peer review day. Bring 2 printed copies of your draft.
Fri Dec 11: Hamlet essay draft due on Turnitin by 11:59pm.
Note: drafts under 3 pages get no peer feedback credit.

== WEEK OF DEC 14 ==
Mon Dec 14: Hamlet unit test (MC + 1 short response).
Wed Dec 16: Mock AP exam, Part 1 (multiple choice, 55 min).
Thu Dec 17: Mock AP exam, Part 2 (3 FRQs, 2 hr) - meets in library, 7:30am start.
Fri Dec 18: Hamlet essay FINAL due on Turnitin by 11:59pm.
Fri Dec 18: Winter reading choice form due (paper form, in class).

== WINTER BREAK (Dec 21 - Jan 3) ==
Read one novel from the winter list; finish by Jan 8.
Winter list: Their Eyes Were Watching God, Things Fall Apart, Jane Eyre, The Remains of the Day, Americanah.
Reading journal: 10 entries, 5 sentences each.
No other assigned work over break.

== AFTER BREAK ==
Fri Jan 8: Winter novel finished, journal due.
Mon Jan 11: In-class discussion on winter novel.
Wed Jan 13: Poetry unit begins.
Fri Jan 22: Timed write #4, poetry analysis.
Fri Jan 29: Semester ends.

== EXTRA CREDIT ==
+2 points on test: attend a school play performance (bring ticket stub).
+3 points on essay: visit the writing center before final submission.
Extra credit capped at 5 points per semester.

== GRADING ==
Essays 35%, tests 25%, timed writes 20%, homework 10%, participation 10%.
Grades update in the portal on Fridays.
Mock AP scores count as a test grade.

Before break you have these deadlines:

- Nov 30: Hamlet Act 3 annotations
- Dec 2: vocab unit 6 quiz
- Dec 4: in-class timed write
- Dec 9: peer review, bring 2 printed copies of your draft
- Dec 11: essay draft on Turnitin by 11:59pm (at least 3 pages, or you get no peer feedback credit)
- Dec 14: Hamlet test
- Dec 16: mock AP multiple choice
- Dec 17: mock AP FRQs in the library, starting at 7:30am
- Dec 18: final essay on Turnitin by 11:59pm, plus the winter reading choice form on paper in class

Over break you only need to read one novel from the winter list and keep a 10-entry journal, both due Jan 8. Late work loses 10% per day, and extra credit (+3 for a writing center visit) is capped at 5 points.

messages.name: fetch_url
messages.content:
Vector Search Libraries on Consumer Hardware: 2026 Benchmark Report
Published 2026-10-14 | Dana Okafor, Min-jun Park | Example Systems Lab

1. Abstract
We benchmark six open-source vector search libraries on laptop-class hardware (Apple M3, 16 GB RAM).
Datasets range from 10k to 5M embeddings at 384 and 768 dimensions.
We measure build time, query latency, recall@10 and peak memory.

2. Libraries tested
FAISS 1.9 (Flat, HNSW, IVF-PQ), hnswlib 0.9, Annoy 1.17, ScaNN 1.4, Chroma 0.6 (embedded), LanceDB 0.14

3. Methodology
Default parameters first, then tuned for recall@10 >= 0.95 where possible.
1,000 random queries per dataset, single thread. Reported values are medians of 5 runs.

4. Results: 50k vectors, 384 dims (build s | p50 ms | recall@10 | peak RAM MB)
FAISS Flat | 0.2 | 3.1 | 1.00 | 95
FAISS HNSW | 9.8 | 0.18 | 0.97 | 160
hnswlib | 7.4 | 0.15 | 0.97 | 140
Annoy | 6.1 | 0.40 | 0.91 | 120
ScaNN | 11.2 | 0.22 | 0.96 | 210
Chroma | 14.5 | 1.9 | 0.96 | 480
LanceDB | 5.3 | 0.9 | 0.95 | 150

5. Results: 1M vectors, 768 dims
FAISS Flat | 1.1 | 118 | 1.00 | 3100
FAISS HNSW | 410 | 0.9 | 0.96 | 4900
hnswlib | 360 | 0.8 | 0.96 | 4400
Annoy | 290 | 2.4 | 0.88 | 3700
ScaNN | 520 | 1.1 | 0.95 | 5600
Chroma | 780 | 6.5 | 0.95 | 9800
LanceDB | 210 | 3.8 | 0.94 | 1900

6. Results: 5M vectors, 768 dims
Only LanceDB (disk-based, 4.1 GB peak) and FAISS IVF-PQ (2.8 GB peak, recall 0.89) finished without swapping.
hnswlib and FAISS HNSW exceeded 16 GB, began swapping, and p50 latency rose above 40 ms.
Chroma ran out of memory at about 3.2M vectors.

7. Usability notes
hnswlib: small API, only save/load of the index file for persistence; no metadata filtering.
FAISS: most flexible, but pip install on Apple silicon needed a conda or pre-built wheel in our tests.
Chroma: embedding functions, metadata filters and persistence out of the box; highest memory use.
LanceDB: on-disk format, metadata filtering and SQL-like queries; slower per query than in-memory graphs.
Annoy: read-only after build; adding vectors requires a rebuild.

8. Limitations
Single machine, single thread, synthetic data plus one public text-embedding dataset. Results on Intel Macs or 8 GB machines may differ.
Recall measured against exact FAISS Flat results.

9. Recommendations
Under 100k vectors: FAISS Flat if you want exact results; hnswlib or FAISS HNSW if latency matters.
100k-1M: hnswlib or LanceDB (if RAM is tight).
Over 1M on 16 GB: LanceDB or FAISS IVF-PQ.
If you need filtering and persistence with minimal code, Chroma is acceptable below ~200k vectors.

Cite as: Okafor, D. & Park, M. (2026). Vector Search Libraries on Consumer Hardware. Example Systems Lab Technical Report ESL-2026-14.

For 50k chunks (the report's 384-dim table), hnswlib is the best fit: 0.15 ms median latency, recall@10 of 0.97, about 140 MB RAM, and 7.4 s to build. FAISS HNSW is nearly identical (0.18 ms, 0.97, 160 MB). If you'd rather have exact results and the simplest setup, FAISS Flat gives recall 1.00 at 3.1 ms, still fast at your size.

Chroma worked (recall 0.96) but used 480 MB and 1.9 ms, so it only makes sense if you want built-in metadata filtering and persistence. hnswlib has no filtering. Two caveats: the tests ran on an M3 single-threaded, and FAISS can be awkward to install on Apple silicon. For your citation, it's Okafor & Park (2026), Example Systems Lab report ESL-2026-14.

can i cite wikipedia in a research paper or nah

Most teachers won't accept it as a source because anyone can edit it and it's a tertiary source. It's fine for getting oriented, though. Check the references at the bottom of the article, then find and cite those original sources instead.
ok and whats the apa format for a website with no author

Start with the page title in place of the author:

Title of page in italics. (Year, Month Day). Site Name. URL

Example: How tides work. (2024, March 5). Ocean Basics. https://www.example.org/tides

If there's no date, use (n.d.). In the text, cite the title in quotes, like ("How Tides Work," 2024).
